title: Putting it together: from the data to a model

diagram.caption: The order of the decisions, from the data to a model
diagram.description: Six numbered steps in a column, each leading to the next. One: check how the data is distributed. Two: choose the hypothesis test. Three: choose one tail or two. Four: compare the test statistic with its curve. Five: weigh the Type I and Type II errors. Six: use the p-value and R-squared to pick the simplest model that works.

meaning: Statistics questions rarely ask for one technique alone. They chain: how the data is spread decides the test, the test decides the curve, and the curve decides what counts as an extreme result.
Analysts care because the exam gives a short scenario and expects you to take the next correct step, so knowing the order helps you spot which step the question is about.
rule: Step 1, the distribution: check whether the data is roughly bell-shaped or skewed, and how big the sample is. This tells you which tests are safe to use.

Step 2, the test: a t-test compares means (a z-test when the population standard deviation is known or the sample is large), chi-squared compares counts in categories, and ANOVA (analysis of variance) compares the means of three or more groups.
Step 3, the tails: the alternative hypothesis sets them. "Lower" means a left tail, "higher" a right tail, and "different" both tails.

Step 4, the test statistic: it says how far the sample is from the null hypothesis, and the curve it is read against changes with the test. The t curve is a bell with heavier tails for small samples, the z curve is the standard bell, and the chi-squared and F curves are skewed and only have a right tail. Compare the statistic with the critical value, or turn it into a p-value.
Step 5, the errors: the significance level α (alpha) is the chance of a Type I error, a false positive. A stricter α lowers that risk but raises the risk of a Type II error, a false negative.

Step 6, the model: when you fit a model, a small p-value for a predictor says its link with the outcome is unlikely to be chance, and R² says how much variation the model explains. Prefer the simplest model that works: extra predictors always nudge R² up, but a model tuned too closely to one sample (overfitting) predicts new data worse.

example.intro: A shop wants to know if a new checkout is faster than the old 60-second average. A sample of 25 customers has a mean of 54 seconds and a sample standard deviation of 15, and the times are roughly bell-shaped. Use α = 0.05.

table.caption: The chain applied to the checkout test
head: Step
Decision
Result
rows: Reject the null; the Type I risk is 5%

steps: The standard error is 15 ÷ √25 = 3, so the sample mean is 2 standard errors below 60.
With two tails the p-value would double to about 0.057, which is above 0.05. The choice of tails changed the answer, so it must come from the question, not from the result.
Step 6, the model: a model with 1 predictor has R² = 0.64, and a model with 9 predictors has R² = 0.66. The extra 8 predictors add only 0.02, so keep the simpler model.

trap.wrong: Choosing the model with the highest R², or choosing the tails after seeing which way the result went.
trap.why: R² never falls when you add predictors, so the highest R² can simply be the most overfitted model. Picking the tails after the fact inflates the Type I error. Decide the tails from the question first, and prefer the simplest model that works.
